structure.title: II. Two-Way Fixed Effects Regressions (decomposition, robustness measures, first-difference extension)
III. An Alternative Estimator (DIDM and placebo estimator)
IV. Extensions (summary of online appendix material)
V.B Application to Gentzkow, Shapiro, and Sinkinson (2011)
V.C The effect of union membership on wages

observations.statement: States that under a single common-trends assumption the two-way fixed effects coefficient identifies a weighted sum of group-period average treatment effects, with weights that need not be positive.
observations.locator: Section I Assumption 5; Section II Theorem 1

observations.statement: Frames treatment-effect heterogeneity across groups and over time, not the usual omitted-variables or endogeneity concern, as the principal threat to interpreting the two-way fixed effects coefficient causally.
Distinguishes sharp designs, where treatment is constant within each group-period cell, from fuzzy designs where it varies within cells, and states that the main text focuses on sharp designs.
observations.note: Fuzzy-design results are relegated to an online appendix that is not available in the extracted text.

observations.statement: Defines staggered adoption designs as a special case of sharp designs in which a group's treatment status is weakly increasing over time, and separately characterizes how negative weighting behaves in that case.

Names a new estimand, the average treatment effect of all cells whose treatment status switches between consecutive periods, and distinguishes it from the average treatment effect on the treated targeted by the standard regressions.

Derives the proposed estimator under a distinct numbered list of assumptions, including strong exogeneity and common trends stated separately for both potential outcomes and an assumption that stable comparison groups exist.

States that its sensitivity ratio only bounds how much treatment-effect heterogeneity would be needed to flip the sign of the regression coefficient, and does not by itself establish that the coefficient is unbiased.
Names the data source for the newspaper application as an existing published dataset covering US presidential elections over a multi-decade period at the county level.
Names the data source for the union-wage application as an existing published panel of young American men, contrasting its sample period with an earlier study that used a different national panel.

Reports the number of observations underlying each estimator directly in the results tables, with counts differing across rows because the new estimator and its placebo variants use different subsamples than the conventional regressions.

Defines outcomes throughout the theoretical sections as group-period cell means rather than individual-level observations, consistent with the paper's notation for the regression coefficients it studies.

Treats the treatment as binary throughout most of the paper, but for the newspaper application generalizes it to a discrete count variable grouped into a small number of categories when computing the new estimator.
Discusses that the union-membership indicator is known from prior literature to be measured with error, and describes a specific rule for recoding single-period reversals in status before estimation.

Reports, separately from the main analysis, that repeating the union analysis on the unrecoded treatment variable changes results little except that one placebo estimator becomes statistically significant.

Documents the fixed-effects structure of the newspaper-application estimators in the table notes rather than in a separate specification row, stating that all reported estimators include state-year fixed effects as controls.
States the clustering level for standard errors directly in each results table's notes, at the county level for the newspaper application and at the worker level for the union-wage application.
Reports point estimate, standard error, and number of observations together in the same row for every estimator shown in the two main results tables.

Stacks the conventional regression estimators and the paper's proposed estimator, along with placebo versions of the latter, as successive rows of one table for each application rather than presenting them in separate tables.

Clusters standard errors by the natural repeated-observation unit in each application (county, worker) without an explicit stated argument for why that level, rather than some other level, was chosen.

Reports that standard errors for the difference between two correlated estimators, such as the conventional and the proposed estimator, are obtained with a clustered bootstrap rather than an analytic formula.

Introduces a placebo estimator, distinct from the standard event-study pretrends test which it argues is invalid under heterogeneous effects, and applies it (with versions lagged two and three periods) to both empirical applications.

Applies the placebo pre-trends estimator to the union-wage application and separately computes it for the subgroups of workers joining and leaving a union, reporting that the placebo differs between the two subgroups.

Reports, for the newspaper application, the share of estimator weights that are negative and their sum, computed with a purpose-built package, as a diagnostic of how binding the negative-weighting problem is.

Computes and reports the correlation between estimator weights and an observed covariate plausibly related to treatment-effect intensity, together with a significance test, as a diagnostic for whether the weights are related to effect heterogeneity.

States that the same negative-weight and sensitivity diagnostics computed for the two applications are recommended more generally to practitioners as a first step before deciding whether to compute the new estimator.

Compares the conventional and proposed estimators for both applications and formally tests whether they differ, treating a significant difference between the conventional level and first-difference estimators as itself evidence against the assumption needed for either to be unbiased.
Reports a robustness check, described in a footnote rather than a main table, comparing results from the recoded and non-recoded treatment variable in the union-wage application.

Separately estimates the treatment effect for the subgroup of units switching into treatment and the subgroup switching out of treatment in the union-wage application, and formally tests whether the two subgroup estimates differ.

Interprets a negative correlation between estimator weights and a worker characteristic as suggestive evidence for why the conventional regression coefficient may overstate the average effect, linking it to a specific explanation from prior literature.

Situates the union-wage regression estimate within existing literature by noting it is close to results from two earlier studies using similar worker-fixed-effects specifications, before introducing the new estimator's results.

Repeatedly reports formal significance tests for whether pairs of estimators differ from one another and treats such differences as informative about the plausibility of identifying assumptions, rather than discussing each estimator's precision only in isolation.

Cautions that the proposed estimator can have larger variance than the conventional two-way fixed effects estimator when the constant-effects model happens to hold, describing a bias-variance trade-off rather than claiming the new estimator strictly dominates.

Notes that its proposed estimator requires the existence of comparison groups whose treatment status is stable between consecutive periods, and reports from its own literature survey that this condition could be confirmed with certainty for only about half of the reviewed papers.

Uses a review of AER-published papers to report how prevalent two-way fixed effects regressions are and how often the condition needed for its estimator plausibly holds, framing this as evidence on the estimator's applicability beyond the two illustrative applications.

Presents a dedicated table of descriptive counts, by estimation method, research-design type, and stable-group status, summarizing the papers identified in its own literature survey rather than summarizing either empirical application's sample.

Reports point estimates with standard errors in an adjacent column in its results tables rather than using significance stars, and instead discusses statistical significance of estimator comparisons narratively via reported t-statistics in the text.

Numbers the survey table reporting counts of papers by year (Table 1) separately from the descriptive-statistics table (Table 2), keeping both survey tables distinct from the two application results tables (Tables 3-4).

Previews the paper's two central results, the negative-weighting decomposition and the new estimator, along with headline qualitative findings from both empirical applications, within the introduction before the formal derivations appear.
Closes the introduction with an explicit roadmap paragraph listing what each numbered section covers, including a pointer to material covered only in a separate online appendix.

Presents the full theoretical framework, decomposition results, and new estimator before introducing any data, turning to sample and data description only in the applications subsection near the end of the paper.

Places proofs of all theorems, propositions, and corollaries in a dedicated appendix after the conclusion, and repeatedly points to a separate online appendix for extensions that are only briefly summarized in the main text.

Includes an explicit paragraph in the introduction stating concrete implications and a decision rule for applied researchers estimating two-way fixed effects regressions, rather than leaving practical recommendations only to the conclusion.

Directs readers in a first-page footnote to the article's online page for additional materials, and the reference list cites a specific replication-data record hosted through an economic-association-affiliated data repository.
Names three purpose-built Stata packages implementing its diagnostics and new estimator, stating they are downloadable together with their help files from a public statistical software archive.
Reuses existing published datasets for both empirical applications rather than collecting new primary data, treating them as illustrative existing studies to which the new estimator is applied.

Sets out a two-step decision rule for applied researchers: first compute the estimator weights and the sensitivity ratio, and only if many weights are negative and the ratio is not large, compute the new estimator instead.

States that Table 1 and Table 2 summarize a review of all papers published in one journal over a three-year window, restricting the count to papers using regressions the authors classify as two-way fixed effects or closely related.

concordance.paper_says: Reports the FE (level) and FD (first-difference) OLS regression estimators for the newspaper-turnout application, computed with state-year fixed effects as controls (Table 3).
concordance.card_shows: Design d2 (Gentzkow_et_al.do): spec s4 is an areg with absorb(cnty90) plus i.year and styr1-styr666 dummies (FE variant); spec s5 is an areg of changeprestout on changedailies with absorb(styr) (FD variant).

concordance.paper_says: Table 3's notes state that standard errors for the newspaper application are clustered by county.
concordance.card_shows: Both s4 and s5 specify cluster(cnty90) in the Stata call.

concordance.paper_says: States that for the newspaper application it also computes its DIDM estimator and a placebo version using the fuzzydid Stata package, adapted for a non-binary treatment.
concordance.card_shows: Gentzkow_et_al.do calls fuzzydid at lines 151-152, but that call falls outside the recipe card's reading budget and is recorded only as an unresolved_reference; no spec or design record captures the fuzzydid estimator for d2.

concordance.paper_says: Table 4's notes state that standard errors for the union-wage application are clustered at the worker level.
concordance.card_shows: Specs s7, s8, and s9 (design d3, from code_unions.do) all specify cluster(nr), where nr is the worker identifier.

concordance.paper_says: Footnotes state that the standard errors of differences between estimators (e.g. the conventional versus the proposed estimator) are obtained with a worker-level clustered bootstrap, distinct from the analytic clustered standard errors reported for each estimator individually.
concordance.card_shows: Spec s9 (did_multiplegt) records se_type as bootstrap with cluster(nr) inside the call; s7 and s8 record se_type as (analytic) cluster.

concordance.paper_says: States that the union-wage application's DIDM estimator, together with three lagged placebo versions, is computed by the did_multiplegt Stata package.
concordance.card_shows: Spec s9: did_multiplegt lwage nr year union, placebo(3) breps(200) cluster(nr), under design d3.

concordance.paper_says: For both applications, compares the conventional FE/FD estimators against the new DIDM estimator and formally tests whether they differ.
concordance.card_shows: Robustness record of type alt_estimator: baseline specs s7, s8 versus variant spec s9 (design d3), relationship_status confirmed.

concordance.paper_says: The main text read (Sections I-VI) does not discuss a population-weighted variant of the fixed-effects regression for either the newspaper or union application.
concordance.card_shows: Robustness record of type alt_se: baseline spec s1 versus variant spec s2, which adds fweight=population1996; both belong to design d1, built from Enikolopov_et_al.do, an application not discussed anywhere in the main text that was read.

concordance.paper_says: States that the two applications revisited in Section V use data from Gentzkow, Shapiro, and Sinkinson (2011) and from Vella and Verbeek (1998); no other dataset or application is named in the main text read.
concordance.card_shows: The card's data records list three source files: voting_cnty_clean.dta (Gentzkow), wagepan.dta (union/Vella-Verbeek), and NTV_Aggregate_Data.dta (Enikolopov et al.), the last of which has no counterpart discussion in the text.

concordance.paper_says: Reports a placebo pre-trends estimator (and lagged variants two and three periods before a treatment switch) for the union-wage application as a check on the common-trends assumption underlying DIDM.
concordance.card_shows: Diagnostic x1: kind=pretrend_test, design d3, spec s9, note '3 placebos', status unknown.

concordance.paper_says: Reports, for the Gentzkow newspaper application (design d2, spec s6, the twowayfeweights call), the share and sum of negative estimator weights as a heterogeneity diagnostic.
concordance.card_shows: Spec s6 (twowayfeweights, design d2) exists but has no diagnostic record attached to it; the card's only heterogeneous_treatment_effects diagnostic (x2) is instead linked to spec s3 under the unrelated Enikolopov design d1.

concordance.paper_says: Does not present a formal covariate balance table for either the newspaper or the union application in the main text read.
concordance.card_shows: Diagnostic x4: kind=balance, design d2, status not_found_in_scope, searched_files=[Gentzkow_et_al.do].

gaps: No balance table is reported for either empirical application; the recipe card independently found no balance check in the code (diagnostic x4, not_found_in_scope).

No explicit stated argument for the choice of clustering level (county for the newspaper application, worker for the union application) beyond the repeated-observation panel structure; no alternative clustering level is discussed.

No preregistration, IRB approval, or consent statement; not applicable, as the paper is a methodological contribution applied to two pre-existing secondary datasets rather than new primary data collection.

The online Appendix (fuzzy-design extensions, non-binary treatment and covariate extensions, consistency proofs under weaker assumptions, and the paper's review of all 33 surveyed AER papers) is referenced repeatedly but is not part of the extracted text, so its content could not be read.
No figures (event-study plots, coefficient plots, binscatters, maps) appear anywhere in the extracted main text; every reported result is presented in a table.

The Enikolopov et al. application present in the paper's replication code (recipe card design d1, specs s1-s3) is not discussed anywhere in the AER-published main text that was read; it may belong to the online appendix or to a dropped draft application.

reading.note: All 33 pages were read, including the introduction, full theoretical sections (I-IV), the applicability survey and both empirical applications (V), the conclusion, and the reference list. The proof appendix (pages 24-32) was skimmed for structure and claims (which theorem each block proves, what is assumed) rather than checked line by line for algebraic correctness, since the note records reporting practice, not correctness. The online Appendix referenced throughout (extensions, additional proofs, review of the 33 surveyed papers) is not part of this extracted text and was not read.
